scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation. Let me start by understanding what's going on here. So, there's this guy, let's call him James, who's 18 years old, and he has a twin sister. He's been best friends with someone named G since kindergarten. That's a really long time, so their friendship is super strong. Now, G and James's sister have had a "thing" going on for a long time, but they never officially dated for various reasons. Eventually, when they were 17, they started dating, and everything was going well for about 13 months. But then, G cheated on James's sister. James found out about the cheating and told his sister, even though G begged him not to. This caused a lot of tension between James and G, and they didn't talk for a month and a half, which was really weird and hard for James because G is like his brother. After that, G invited James on his family ski trip to make amends, and James accepted. They ended up forgiving each other, and James let G back into his life because it was too weird without him. James can tell that G is genuinely sorry, and G even cried because he felt so bad. Now, G and James's sister broke up after the cheating was discovered, and they're not speaking anymore. James's sister is upset with him for still being friends with G and is making him feel bad about it. She doesn't understand why their 13-year friendship is so important to him, especially over her. James feels that G made a huge mistake, and he hates him for it, but he doesn't want to lose his best friend over this. He's trying to rationalize it by thinking that if his best friend cheated on their significant other, he wouldn't end the friendship, so why should this situation be any different just because the significant other is his sister? They're also planning to go to the same college in the fall, which is in a different state from where his sister is going, so he thinks this whole situation won't be a big deal once they're all in different places. Now, the question is: Am I the asshole? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider a few things. First, what defines being the asshole in this context? It seems like the main issue is whether James is justified in continuing his friendship with G despite G cheating on James's sister. Is it fair for James to prioritize his friendship with G over his sister's feelings? Or is James being too lenient with G, considering the betrayal involved? Let's break it down. On one hand, James has known G for a really long time, and their friendship is very important to him. He's been through a lot with G, and losing that friendship would be devastating. He also points out that if his best friend cheated on someone else, he wouldn't end the friendship, so why should this situation be any different? That seems like a valid point because the betrayal is the same, regardless of who the significant other is. On the other hand, his sister feels betrayed and hurt, and she's upset with him for not taking her side. She feels like James is prioritizing his friendship with G over her feelings, which is understandable. Being cheated on is a deeply personal and painful experience, and it's natural for her to want James to support her by cutting ties with G. Another angle to consider is the impact on G. G has shown genuine remorse, cried, and made an effort to make amends by inviting James on the ski trip. James has forgiven him and let him back into his life. This suggests that G has taken responsibility for his actions and is working to repair the relationship. However, does this forgiveness extend to the relationship with James's sister? It seems like G and James's sister are not speaking, so the issue between them remains unresolved. Also, the fact that James and G are planning to go to the same college in a different state might mean that the situation will naturally fade into the background as they move on with their lives. This could be a positive aspect because it might allow everyone to move past the incident without it overshadowing their futures. But then, there's the question of loyalty. Should James stand by his sister, especially since she's his twin and they're so close? Or is it reasonable for him to maintain his friendship with G, given the long history and the effort G has made to apologize? I think it's also important to consider the dynamics of the relationships involved. James has a unique position because he's both G's best friend and his sister's brother. This puts him in the middle of a difficult situation where he has to balance his loyalty to both. It's not easy, and there's no clear right or wrong answer because both sides have valid feelings and perspectives. In the end, whether James is the asshole depends on how one views the importance of friendship versus loyalty to family, especially in the face of betrayal. If one prioritizes long-term friendships and the effort to repair relationships, then James might not be the asshole. However, if one believes that loyalty to family and supporting them through betrayal is more important, then James could be seen as the asshole for not taking his sister's side. It's a tough spot to be in, and there's no perfect solution. James has to weigh his own feelings, his friendship with G, and his relationship with his sister, and decide what he thinks is the right thing to do based on his values and priorities.
